Problem 10 Dearomatization of Benzene Rings (27 points, 13%)
Aromaticity makes the benzene ring structurally stable and provides substantial resonance stabilization. Directly disrupting its aromatic conjugation or cleaving a C–C bond in the ring framework normally requires considerable energy. Dearomatization or ring-opening cleavage of a benzene ring is therefore highly challenging.

subquestions.text_open:
10.1 In 2024, researchers developed a novel benzene-ring-opening strategy that directly converts a range of aryl azide derivatives into valuable multiply conjugated enynes.
10.1.1 Write the SMILES string for intermediate A formed before $^tBuONa$ is added.

text_images.description: Single-step reaction: 'O=C(C1=CC=CC=C1N=[N+]=[N-])C2=CC=CC=C2'>TosNHNH2 (1.2 equiv), TFA (20 mol%), PhCl (0.2 M); then $^tBuONa$ (1.5 equiv), PhCl (0.1 M), 130°C>'N#C/C=C\C=C/C#CC1=CC=CC=C1'.

rubric: A: '[N-]=[N+]=NC1=CC=CC=C1/C(C2=CC=CC=C2)=N/NS(C3=CC=C(C)C=C3)(=O)=O' (1 point; E/Z geometry of the double bond is not required)

10.1.2 To investigate the mechanism, the researchers performed the following experiments.
Calculations indicate that after $^tBuONa$ is added, loss of one molecule of gas first produces highly reactive intermediate B. B then reacts with the azide group to form charge-separated tricyclic intermediate C. A concerted reaction of C expels another gas molecule to give the product. Write the SMILES strings for B and C.

text_images.description: Two parallel mechanistic experiments. Upper reaction: the starting material is labeled only A and its structure is not drawn; conditions are TEMPO (2.0 equiv), $^tBuONa$ (1.5 equiv), PhCl, heat, giving 'N#C/C=C\C=C/C#CC1=CC=CC=C1' in 70% yield. rubric: B: '[N-]=[N+]=NC1=CC=CC=C1[C]C2=CC=CC=C2' (1 point); C: '[N-]=[N+]1C(C2=CC=CC=C2)=C(C=CC=C3)C3=N1' (2 points). Reasonable resonance forms of B and C also receive credit.

subquestions.text_open:
10.2.2 The researchers reacted differently substituted nitroarenes with a substrate containing both an aromatic ring and an alkene and found that the substituents affect chemoselectivity. For example, nitroarenes N1 and N2 react with D to give selective oxidation of either the alkene or the aromatic ring.
Studies of nitroarene excited states show that their lowest triplet state may have either a $^3(n,\pi^*)$ or $^3(\pi,\pi^*)$ electronic configuration. These correspond, respectively, to an n to $\pi^*$ transition, representable as a dioxygen-diradical species, and a $\pi, \pi^*$ transition, involving intramolecular electron transfer from the benzene unit to the nitro group with the unpaired electron delocalized over the entire $\pi$ system. Based on the electronic properties of the substituents, which state is lower in energy for N1, and which is lower for N2?
(a) n, $\pi^*$ state; (b) $\pi, \pi^*$ state.

text_images.description: Three compounds, labeled D, N1, and N2 from left to right. The SMILES for N1 is 'O=[N+](C1=CC=C(OC)C(OC)=C1)[O-]'; for N2, 'O=[N+](C1=CC(C(F)(F)F)=CC(C(F)(F)F)=C1)[O-]'; and for D, 'C/C(C)=C\CCOC1=CC=CC2=C1C=CC=C2'.

rubric: (b), (a) (2 points only if both are correct)

subquestions.text_open:
10.2.3 A triplet excited state with an n, $\pi^*$ configuration can undergo cycloaddition directly. A triplet excited state with a $\pi, \pi^*$ configuration cannot undergo direct concerted cycloaddition; calculations indicate the following pathway. It first forms a complex with the other substrate, in which dispersion is the principal intermolecular attraction. Partial electron transfer between the substrates then gives the nitro group a partial negative charge and the other substrate a partial positive charge, promoting formation of the first C–O bond. Finally, intersystem crossing and ring closure give the five-membered intermediate. Accordingly, a nitroarene excited state with an n, $\pi^*$ configuration reacts more readily with (   ), whereas one with a $\pi, \pi^*$ configuration reacts more readily with (   ). Explain each choice.
(a) An electron-rich aromatic ring; (b) an isolated double bond.
rubric: (b), (a) (2 points only if both are correct. Award no explanation points for an incorrect choice; likewise, a correct choice without the corresponding correct explanation receives no explanation credit.)

n, $\pi^*$ configuration: cycloaddition to an aromatic ring would destroy aromaticity and therefore has a high activation energy, so the n, $\pi^*$ nitroarene excited state reacts more readily with an isolated double bond (1 point for mentioning the difficulty of disrupting aromaticity).

$\pi, \pi^*$ configuration: an aromatic ring has a larger polarizable $\pi$ surface and broader contact area than an isolated alkene bond, providing stronger dispersion and favoring complex formation. An electron-rich aromatic ring also transfers an electron to the nitro group more readily than an isolated double bond because its HOMO is higher (2 points: 1 for stronger dispersion and 1 for the charge-transfer complex).

10.3 In 2024, Professor Youliang Wang's group achieved thermochemical dearomatization of a benzene ring, constructing a complex ring system in one step.
Experiments show that when TFA is replaced by deuterated TFA and the reaction is run for 10 h, 99% of the circled hydrogen atom in the product is replaced by deuterium.
10.3.1 The reaction includes a pericyclic step. Write the SMILES strings for 3–4 key intermediates and name the pericyclic reaction.

text_images.description: Single-step reaction: 'C=CCN(C1=CC=CC=C1)C(C#CC2=CC=CC=C2)=O'>TFA, 50°C, 12h>'O=C(N1C2)C([H])=C(C31C4C5C=CC3C2C4)C6=C5C=CC=C6'. The hydrogen at C([H]) in the product is circled, corresponding to the deuterium-labeling experiment in the prompt.

rubric: Intermediate 1: 'O=C1N(CC=C)C2(C=CC=C[CH+]2)C(C3=CC=CC=C3)=C1[H]'; intermediate 2: 'O=C(N1C2)C([H])=C([C@@]31[C@H]4[CH+]C=C[C@@H]3C2C4)C5=CC=CC=C5'; intermediate 3: 'O=C1C([H])=C2C3=CC=C[CH+]C3C4C=CC5C62C4CC5CN16' (2 points each; award credit if connectivity is correct and the charge is represented reasonably. Consider only the first 4 intermediates drawn by the student).
An intermediate formed by addition of $H^+$ to the triple bond receives neither credit nor a penalty.

rubric_images.description: Three cationic intermediates, from left to right. Intermediate 1 has SMILES 'O=C1N(CC=C)C2(C=CC=C[CH+]2)C(C3=CC=CC=C3)=C1[H]'; intermediate 2, 'O=C(N1C2)C([H])=C([C@@]31[C@H]4[CH+]C=C[C@@H]3C2C4)C5=CC=CC=C5'; intermediate 3, 'O=C1C([H])=C2C3=CC=C[CH+]C3C4C=CC5C62C4CC5CN16'.

The SMILES for the intermediate formed by addition of $H^+$ to the triple bond is 'C=CCN(C1=CC=CC=C1)C(/C([H])=[C+]/C2=CC=CC=C2)=O'. The positive charge is at [C+]. The rubric specifies that drawing this intermediate earns no credit but incurs no penalty.
